transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-11
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Quasar - Head of Security), Rajiv Menon (Quasar - Cloud Architect), Sofia Alvarez (Quasar - Compliance), Tom Becker (Quasar - DevOps)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Quick security review to align on encryption posture and options for BYOK/HSM for Quasar's private cluster. Discussed audit logs, RBAC/SSO, and a tentative on-prem trial.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick roll call please?
[00:06] Lena (Quasar): Lena here.
[00:07] Rajiv: Rajiv on the call.
[00:09] Sofia: Sofia.
[00:10] Tom: Tom here.
[00:11] Omar (Redwood SE): Omar, hi. Jordan too?
[00:13] Jordan: Jordan, yep.
[00:15] Maya: Great. Goal for today is twofold: make sure we understand Quasar's encryption requirements end-to-end and cover practical onboarding options for BYOK and HSM, including provenance and operational runbooks.
[00:27] Lena: Sounds good. We're under a mandate to have customer-controlled keys for sensitive PII workloads. SOC 2 is in flight but we also have ISO efforts, so we need clear chain-of-custody for keys and audit logs.
[00:40] Omar: Understood. Before we deep-dive, quick framing — Redwood supports hosted KMS, a dedicated BYOK connector to customer KMS, and an on-prem HSM integration. Each has tradeoffs on latency, availability, and control.
[00:53] Rajiv: If you could put those tradeoffs in plain terms; my team cares about throughput for inference bursts and predictable tail latency.
[01:02] Jordan: Right, tradeoffs are basically: managed cloud KMS is simplest but keys leave customer's direct custody; BYOK with cloud KMS keeps you in control of key material but still imposes network calls; HSM (FIPS 140-2/3) on premises gives the strongest provable control but adds ops complexity and potential network hop to the runtime.
[01:22] Lena: And we need to document that for auditors — show that keys were generated under our KMS/HSM and the provider can't export them.
[01:30] Omar: For HSMs we support sealed keys + PKCS#11 and can integrate with common vendors. We also do key-wrapping (envelope encryption) so the per-token encryption key is wrapped by the customer key, which never leaves the HSM.
[01:45] Tom: Can you clarify envelope encryption in your runtime? Will the runtime request unwrapped keys during inference and store KV cache?
[01:54] Omar: Good question. We never persist unwrapped customer master keys to disk; runtime uses a short-lived data key cached in memory and uses in-memory KV cache for the session. We do prefix/KV cache — excuse me the transcriber sometimes says KV 'cash' — it's actually KV cache and we enforce memory-only storage for unwrapped keys.
[02:15] Rajiv: How do you handle rotation? We need to rotate master keys quarterly and also keep ability to re-encrypt existing blobs.
[02:24] Jordan: We support key versioning. Rotation workflow is: create new key in HSM/KMS, release a new wrapping key version, update runtime to request the new wrapped key. For existing encrypted blobs, we support lazy re-wrap on access or a bulk rewrap job. We can provide a rewrap playbook.
[02:40] Sofia: For audit we need provable history — who requested key, what IP, and the operation (encrypt/decrypt). Does Redwood surface those events?
[02:49] Omar: Yes. Our audit logs include requestor identity (federated via SSO), request timestamp, operation, request payload metadata (redacted), and the model/version used. Logs are retained per your chosen retention policy and can be exported to your SIEM. Note that if you use a third-party HSM, HSM vendor logs are separate — we link events via key IDs.
[03:10] Lena: What's the SSO mapping? We use Okta with SAML and groups-based RBAC — we need separation of duties between ops and security.
[03:18] Maya: We integrate with SAML SSO; group attributes map to Redwood roles. You can create RBAC policies that restrict who can do key operations (create/rotate/escape) — small aside the transcriber mis-says escape, we mean 'export' — export is never allowed for non-admins unless you use key escrow.
[03:37] Rajiv: Key escrow — does Redwood offer escrow? We were told there's an escrow flow for disaster recovery.
[03:44] Omar: We do an optional escrow/escrow agent pattern. For BYOK, the customer chooses whether to escrow a copy (encrypted) to a sealed escrow store — usually for compliance teams only. Many customers prefer no escrow; it's opt in.
[03:56] Tom: For the HSM on-prem option, what's the network topology? We want to avoid cross-region egress for data plane.
[04:04] Jordan: Two main patterns: colocated HSM in the same VPC where the inference runtime lives (low latency) or an HSM behind a customer gateway that the runtime reaches over a private peering link. We recommend co-location for latency-sensitive inference.
[04:20] Sofia: Can you produce a diagram of the peering path and the audit event flow?
[04:24] Maya: Absolutely, Omar will share a network/integration diagram and checklist after the call.
[04:30] [00:04:31] Lena: Regarding regulatory residency — our EU customers' PII must stay in EU regions. If we bring our own HSM, does Redwood's control plane see key material?
[04:41] Omar: Control plane metadata is visible (key ID, creation timestamp, versions) but not key material. If you run Private with on-prem HSM option, the KMS operations can be proxied directly to your HSM so Redwood never sees unwrapped keys. For hosted BYOK there's still metadata in control plane but material stays in your KMS/HSM.
[04:58] Rajiv: How are keys transported during initial provisioning? We want a secure key handshake and not paste keys over email.
[05:06] Jordan: We support a secure provisioning protocol — either an offline import via HSM vendor tooling (for on-prem HSM) or an API-based wrapped-key import where you generate the key in your KMS, wrap it with a Redwood-provided ephemeral public key, and upload the wrapped blob. We document this in the integration checklist.
[05:25] Tom: Does Redwood support HSMs that are FIPS + Common Criteria validated?
[05:30] Omar: Yes, we have integrations tested with mainstream FIPS 140-2/3 validated modules (vendor names in the checklist). We also provide requirements for HSM firmware and PKCS#11 versions.
[05:40] [00:05:41] Sofia: Auditors will ask for evidence of key provenance — a chain showing the key generation, wrapped import, and rotations. Can Redwood provide structured export for that?
[05:50] Omar: We can export a signed provenance report showing key creation metadata and the wrapping events. If you have an HSM that signs operations, we can include those signatures in the artifact. There's some vendor variance but generally yes.
[06:03] Lena: Any caveats around latency/throughput when you do HSM calls per-token?
[06:09] Jordan: We do envelope encryption: per-token we use a fast symmetric data key. HSM calls happen for unwrap/wrap events on session start/rotation. So runtime calls to HSM are amortized; not per token. For bursty inference the KV cache reduces HSM call rate.
[06:24] Rajiv: What about quantization or model caching — any implications for decrypting model weights or storing them unencrypted?
[06:31] Omar: Model weights are stored encrypted at rest; the model loader decrypts into memory. We support FIPS-mode for crypto libraries if needed. The keys for at-rest model encryption are also wrapped by customer master keys when BYOK configured.
[06:46] [00:06:47] Tom: Are audit logs tamper-evident? We need immutable journaling for compliance.
[06:52] Maya: Logs can be exported to your SIEM and also to an append-only storage with WORM settings. We sign events server-side; we can provide hashing chain proofs on request.
[07:03] Sofia: For SOC 2 they also want role separation — can we block admin-level key rotation to one group and have another group approve it?
[07:12] Omar: You can require a two-person approval for key rotation via RBAC + an approval workflow that hooks into a ticketing system. We have an API to enforce preconditions before rotation. We'll include an example policy in the playbook.
[07:25] Lena: Are there examples of customers that have done on-prem HSM with Redwood?
[07:29] Maya: Yes, a few financial customers and a healthcare provider. We can redact specifics but will provide anonymized architecture references and the audit artifacts we supplied.
[07:39] Rajiv: How about disaster recovery — if an HSM fails, what's the recovery path?
[07:45] Jordan: Standard options: (1) use key escrow (encrypted) stored in a geographically separate vault, (2) keep a rotated secondary key in another HSM, or (3) pre-authorized emergency unwrap via multi-sig escrow. We can show recovery runbooks.
[07:59] Tom: We need to validate PKCS#11 compatibility. Any notes on versions or quirks?
[08:05] Omar: We'll include PKCS#11 version compat matrix. Some vendors have quirks around slot indexing and session limits — the checklist calls out concurrent session tuning.
[08:20] [00:08:21] Sofia: A slightly separate ask — how do you handle telemetry that might be considered sensitive? For example, model prompts that include PII.
[08:29] Maya: We redact user-provided prompt content in logs by default and only retain high-level metadata unless you opt-in to store full transcripts for evaluation. For private deployments you can disable telemetry entirely.
[08:42] Rajiv: For on-prem HSM, will Redwood agents run in our VPC or do you require outbound to Redwood control plane?
[08:50] Jordan: For Private mode the control plane can be customer-hosted or a minimal control-plane endpoint that only stores metadata. We support a customer VPC connector so agents run in your VPC; only heartbeat and metadata reach Redwood control plane, encrypted in transit.
[09:05] Omar: Quick note on certificate management — we support mTLS for service-to-service and recommend mutual auth between runtime and HSM gateway.
[09:15] Lena: Any regulatory flags for cross-border key wrapping?
[09:19] Maya: If keys or wrapped artifcats transit outside region, some regulations flag that. The recommended approach is to keep HSM and wrapping operations within the region for PII workloads. We'll call out specifics per jurisdiction in the security brief.
[09:31] [00:09:32] Rajiv: About cost — HSM endpoints and operations have cost. Is pricing per unwrap/operation or a flat add-on?
[09:39] Maya: Pricing model can be a dedicated BYOK add-on plus per-hour reservation for dedicated capacity and optional per-operation charge for hardware HSM operations if vendor billing applies. Maya: we'll send ranges.
[09:55] Sofia: For auditing, we also need to show retention and deletion policies for keys and for the wrapped data keys used in caching.
[10:03] Jordan: Keys: master keys are retained as per your KMS policy; wrapped data keys we keep transiently as per session TTL and they are rotated and deleted per retention settings. We record deletion events in the audit log.
[10:18] [00:10:19] Tom: Any testing we should run during pilot to validate SLOs?
[10:23] Omar: Yes, we recommend three tests: (1) cold-start latency with HSM wrap/unwarp, (2) sustained throughput with KV cache enabled, (3) failover tests where HSM is temporarily unavailable and runtime falls back to cached keys or uses a secondary key policy. We'll send a benchmark spreadsheet.
[10:40] Rajiv: About fallbacks — if HSM is down, do you fail open or fail closed?
[10:45] Jordan: Default is fail closed for decrypt operations to preserve confidentiality, but you can configure graceful degradation: cached session keys allow short-term operation, or a secondary key policy with stricter auditing. We'll document tradeoffs.
[10:59] Lena: We want to ensure the audit trail captures when failover happened and who authorized it.
[11:04] Omar: We'll log failover events and require an authorized actor to trigger a fallback if you enable manual approval in the policy.
[11:14] Maya: We're coming up on time. Quick recap of agreed items?
[11:18] Lena: We want the HSM integration checklist, the PKCS#11 matrix, a provenance report sample, and an anonymized customer reference. Also pricing.
[11:26] Maya: Yes. Omar will share the technical checklist and the sample provenance report. I'll follow up on pricing ranges and pilot scheduling.
[11:33] Sofia: We'll confirm the residency list and the internal stakeholders who will be on the pilot.
[11:37] Tom: We'll run through the PKCS#11 env and gather firmware versions.
[11:41] Maya: Great. Any final questions?
[11:44] Rajiv: One quick thing — do you support HSM key attestation for hardware provenance?
[11:49] Omar: Yes, attestation is supported where the HSM vendor exposes attestation APIs; we can capture attestation metadata in the provenance export.
[11:58] [00:11:59] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send notes and the checklist by Wednesday next week.
[12:05] [crosstalk] 
[12:07] Lena: Thanks. Bye.

--- End of transcript ---
